questions.question: Which two parts of the human eye act as convex lenses that together provide enough optical power to focus images of faraway objects on the retina?
options: The cornea and the retina
The cornea and the natural lens
The natural lens and the vitreous fluid
The aqueous fluid and the vitreous fluid
questions.explanation: The eye effectively contains two convex lenses: the cornea and the natural lens. Their combined optical power focuses faraway objects onto the retina.

questions.question: Compared with an artificial lens setup, what feature of the human eye replaces a focal plane?
options: Its liquid-filled vitreous fluid
Its flat focal plane behind the cornea
Its variable-power natural lens
Its non-planar, spherically curved retina
questions.explanation: The human eye has no focal plane as such. Its non-planar, spherically curved retina replaces the focal plane.

questions.question: What is the main role of the convex lens in a VR headset when the screen is placed very close to the eye?
options: To let the screen fill the eye's field
To focus the screen's light on the retina
To increase the visible pixel count
To replace the eye's natural lens
questions.explanation: A VR headset uses a convex lens, like reading glasses, to focus the close screen's light on the retina. After that, normal eye operation takes over.

questions.question: Why is the screen in a VR headset placed at the focal length of its engineered lens for the best experience?
options: So the screen's light can pass only through air
So the user's natural lens can be bypassed
So the screen appears as an enormous virtual image at an infinite distance
So a real image is formed in front of the user's face
questions.explanation: Placing the screen at the focal length makes it appear to the user as an enormous virtual image at an infinite distance.

questions.question: Although a VR headset screen can appear to the user as a virtual image, what must happen for the person to perceive it?
options: A virtual image must be formed on the retina
A flat pixel grid must be projected onto the retina
A real image must be formed on the retina
A stereoscopic image must be formed in the air
questions.explanation: In a VR headset, a real image is nevertheless formed on the retina. A person does not perceive the world unless real images are formed on the retina.

questions.question: What is the field of view (FOV) in visual perception?
options: A linear measure of the distance to visible objects
An angular measure of the region visible at a single point in time
A count of the objects visible at a single point in time
A fixed property of a display screen's size
questions.explanation: FOV is the view frustum, that is, the region visible to the human eye, and it is measured angularly at one point in time.

questions.question: When both eyes focus on infinity in binocular vision, what is seen in the common region?
options: Only the right eye sees the common region
The left and right eyes see two completely different images
Only the left eye sees the common region
The same image is seen by both eyes
questions.explanation: In binocular vision, both eyes see the same image over a common region when focusing on infinity.

questions.question: How does binocular vision support perception of three-dimensional space?
options: It enhances depth perception and relationships between objects
It increases the angular width of the field of view
It makes the retina act as a flat focal plane
It replaces peripheral vision with central vision
questions.explanation: Binocular vision enhances depth perception and helps a person understand relationships between objects in 3D space.

questions.question: In stereoscopy, how are the two images assigned to the eyes?
options: Both eyes process only the right image
The left eye processes the right image and the right eye processes the left image
The left eye processes the left image and the right eye processes the right image
Both eyes process only the left image
questions.explanation: Stereoscopy involves the left eye processing the left image and the right eye processing the right image simultaneously.

questions.question: What result is produced when the left and right 2D images are processed simultaneously in stereoscopy?
options: A single flat two-dimensional image
Only the right two-dimensional image
Only the left two-dimensional image
A three-dimensional view of the objects
questions.explanation: Simultaneous processing of the left and right 2D images generates a 3D view, helping stereoscopic vision perceive 3D objects.

questions.question: What is translational movement used for in a virtual world?
options: Moving at different angles along the translational axis
Mapping the environment while localizing positions in it
Navigating in the three-dimensional virtual space
Aligning a real-world region with a virtual region
questions.explanation: Translational movement is used for navigating in three-dimensional space, while rotational movement is used for moving at different angles along the translational axis.

questions.question: What does the term degrees of freedom describe?
options: The different ways an object can move in space
The simultaneous mapping and locating of a real environment
The process of seeing two images at the same time
The region visible to the human eye at one time
questions.explanation: Degrees of freedom indicate the different ways an object can move in space.

questions.question: In three-dimensional space, an object's degrees of freedom are divided into which two groups?
options: Rotational and translational degrees of freedom
Translational and navigational degrees of freedom
Rotational and visual degrees of freedom
Rotational and binocular degrees of freedom
questions.explanation: In 3D space, an object has six degrees of freedom: three rotational degrees of freedom and three translational degrees of freedom.

questions.question: In a virtual world, motion is perceived with respect to which factor?
options: The supported degrees of freedom
The pixels per square area of a display
The human eye's horizontal field of view
The real-world region where virtual content aligns
questions.explanation: Motion in a virtual world is perceived with respect to the degrees of freedom that are supported.

questions.question: Which three display characteristics are highlighted as important for making a VR display match human visual sense?
options: Spatial resolution, temporal resolution, and color gamut
Spatial resolution, intensity resolution and range, and temporal resolution.
Spatial resolution, field of view, and intensity resolution
Intensity resolution, frame rate, and field of view
questions.explanation: The important considerations for matching the human visual sense are spatial resolution, intensity resolution and range, and temporal resolution.

questions.question: What does aliasing refer to in a display?
options: An image appearing to have a screen-like grid over it
The minimum pixel density needed for a display to be called a retina display
A frame rate too low to make displayed motion appear smooth
A sharp diagonal line appearing jagged when individual display lights are visible.
questions.explanation: Aliasing is the perception of a sharp diagonal line as jagged or staircase-shaped when individual display lights are visible.

questions.question: Why is the usual distant-display retina resolution criterion less suitable for VR headsets?
options: AR displays are close to the eye, so the distant-display criterion is too high
VR headsets rely on LCD projectors, which produce a screen door effect
VR displays need lower pixel density because immersive motion needs higher frame rates
A magnifying lens places the display close to the eye, increasing required pixel density.
questions.explanation: For displays close to the eye, such as VR headsets, the traditional distant-display retina criterion is not very suitable because a magnifying lens brings the display close to the eye, requiring much higher pixel density.

questions.question: Besides increasing spatial resolution, what method can help reduce aliasing or screen door effect in VR headsets?
options: Increasing the number of producible intensity values
Lowering frame rates to ordinary television or movie standards
Designing the display to be used at a distance from the eye
Adjusting field of view or using foveated rendering.
questions.explanation: Corrective mechanisms include adjusting field of view, foveated rendering, and other content-rendering approaches, in addition to increasing spatial resolution.

questions.question: What does motion perception in an immersive VR environment require of temporal resolution?
options: A frame rate determined by the display's spatial resolution
Frame rates comparable to ordinary television or movie standards
Frame rates much higher than ordinary television or movie standards.
Only a frame rate high enough to avoid diagonal-line aliasing
questions.explanation: Temporal resolution for VR motion perception requires frame rates much higher than ordinary television or movie standards, with higher frame rates preferred.

questions.question: How does a virtual reality headset use its engineered lens and close screen to make a virtual image that the eye still perceives as a real visual scene?
questions.reference_answer: A virtual reality headset places a screen very close to the eyes and uses a convex lens to focus the screen's light on the retina. For the best experience, the screen is placed at the focal length of the engineered lens, so the screen appears as an enormous virtual image at an infinite distance. Even though the user perceives a virtual image, a real image is nevertheless formed on the retina, and perception requires real images on the retina.

questions.question: Why can two flat two-dimensional images shown to the left and right eyes produce a three-dimensional view in an immersive display?
questions.reference_answer: In binocular vision, when both eyes focus on infinity, they see the same image over a common region of about 120 degrees, while areas outside that region are seen by only one eye. In stereoscopy, the left eye processes the left two-dimensional image and the right eye processes the right two-dimensional image. When those images are processed simultaneously, the result is a three-dimensional view; this stereoscopic vision, aided by binocular vision, helps perceive three-dimensional objects and enhances depth perception of object relationships in three-dimensional space.

questions.question: Why is the 326 pixels per linear inch retina display criterion useful for some augmented reality experiences but not for virtual reality headsets or other wearable displays close to the eye?
questions.reference_answer: A retina display is defined as a display with a minimum resolution of 326 pixels per linear inch. Because augmented reality experiences are typically experienced using displays at a distance from the eye, that criterion can be taken into account for distant displays. For augmented reality head-mounted displays, virtual reality headsets, or other wearable displays close to the eye, a magnifying lens brings the display close to the eye, so the required pixels per linear inch is probably 7 to 8 times higher than the retina display criterion.

questions.question: How do supported degrees of freedom in a virtual world connect to the frame-rate requirements for motion perception in an immersive environment?
questions.reference_answer: In three-dimensional space, an object can have six degrees of freedom: yaw, roll, and pitch rotation, plus movement along the x, y, and z axes. A virtual world may allow translational movement for navigating in three-dimensional space and rotational movement for moving at different angles, and motion is perceived with respect to the degrees of freedom that are supported. Temporal resolution is the frame rate, and it must allow motion to be perceived smoothly without jitter; for motion perception in an immersive environment, a virtual reality headset requires frame rates much higher than ordinary television or movie standards such as 24 frames per second or 60 frames per second.
